t: a courtyard. An open area surrounded by partitions onto which several houses open.

for the entire courtyard is one private domain. Any place surrounded by partitions ten handbreadths high is considered a private domain, even if it is a large area and even if many people live in it (see Hilchot Shabbat 14:1).

and the same law applies to an alley that has a side-post or a beam. A lane leading off the public domain onto which a number of courtyards open; carrying in it is not prohibited if a side-post (a post ten handbreadths high) was placed at its entrance or a beam was passed over its entrance (see ibid. 17:2).
in a city. A town.
by rabbinic law. By enactment of the Sages.
that is divided into residences. That has separate residents.
a camp. One fixed in place.
a caravan. One moving from place to place.
for they are all mixed together and those are not fixed tents of theirs. They are considered as having combined because their dwelling is only temporary, and no tent is a domain unto itself.
just as it is permitted to carry out from the courtyards to the streets and markets of the city. In a case where the entire city is surrounded by a wall.
and they will think that carrying out is not a forbidden labor. They will mistakenly think that moving an object from one domain to another is not a labor forbidden on Shabbat.
that it be divided into residences, and each one holds in it a domain of his own. Each person has his own dwelling in it.
a place in the possession of all of them, in which the hand of all is equal. A shared area that everyone has the right to use.
such as a courtyard of houses. The courtyard is a domain shared by all the residents of the houses.
that is to say. As an expression of this.
and by this act. Of placing the eruv.
a loaf baked from a se'ah, and it is sliced. A large loaf made from a se'ah of flour (about seven liters), and it is cut.
if it was whole and is the size of an issar. Small, like the coin called an issar.
millet. A kind of legume. Since it is not customary to make bread from it, one may not make an eruv with it.
like muries. A drink meant for dipping.
the size of a dried fig. The size of a fig.
as much as six average eggs. About 300 cc.
as it is. By itself.
and raw meat. For some people are accustomed to eat it so (Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 3:1).
a relish. Food eaten together with bread.
and the mother-bulbs of onions. Onions left in the ground and used for seed.
enough to eat two meals with it. An amount eaten with bread in the quantity of two meals.
in undiluted wine. Not mixed with water.
revi'iyot. A quarter of a log (about seventy-five cc).
a litra... an ukla... a kav... a maneh. Measures of volume (their quantities are detailed in the following halachot).

boiled soft. Lightly cooked in water without spices (note of Rabbi Y. Kafih on Commentary to the Mishnah Berakhot 6:8; see also Commentary to the Mishnah Terumot 10:11, Hilchot Nedarim 9:1). Some explain that shaluk means cooked a great deal (Rashi, Nedarim 49a and others; and see Meiri there, that the word is interpreted in both senses, depending on the context).
cooked and not cooked. Partly cooked.
dried fig cake. Dried figs.
hops... chazin. Kinds of plants.
beans. A kind of legume.
they sprouted. They grew.
and likewise anything similar to them. For any food that is a relish, one estimates by the amount one eats of it together with two meals of bread.
a hundred dinars. About 480 grams.
and we have already explained the measure of a revi'it and its weight. In the previous halacha (for another definition see Hilchot Bikkurim 6:15).
and these are the measures that a person must always remember. For details on this, see the supplements: 'Torah measures and quantities'.
a nazirite may join in wine. Even though he is forbidden to drink wine (Hilchot Nezirut 5:1-2).
and a Israelite in terumah. Even though a non-priest is forbidden to eat terumah (Hilchot Terumot 6:5).
tevel. Produce from which terumah and tithes have not been separated (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:19).
tevel by rabbinic law. Produce from which the obligation to separate terumah and tithes is by rabbinic law.
first tithe whose terumah was not taken properly. The terumah of the tithe, and sometimes also the great terumah (see Hilchot Terumot 3:13).
second tithe and consecrated property that were not redeemed properly. For the proper manner of redemption see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni chapter 4, Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin chapter 7.
in demai. Produce of ordinary people (amei ha-aretz) about which it is not known whether it was tithed; the Sages instituted that tithes be separated from it out of doubt (Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1).
because it is fit for the poor. Demai may be eaten by the poor (see ibid. 10:11), and therefore with regard to everyone it is considered food with no prohibition in it.

for the added fifth is not indispensable. By law, one who redeems second tithe or consecrated property adds a fifth to the redemption money. But the sanctity is removed even if he did not add it, and although initially he should not eat or benefit until he gives the fifth, it is considered food with no prohibition in it (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 5:12, Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 7:3).
in second tithe. The tithe separated after the first tithe, which is eaten in Jerusalem (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1).
in the outlying areas. Anywhere other than Jerusalem.
in a storehouse. A warehouse.
if he put it in a gatehouse... it is not an eruv. The eruv must be placed in a house, and these places are not considered a house (compare Hilchot Mezuzah 6:7).
in a gatehouse. A booth next to the gate of the house in which the doorkeeper sits.
in a portico. An open area in front of the house that has three walls and a roof.

and a house in which the eruv is placed need not give bread. The purpose of placing the eruv in a particular house is to express that the residents of the courtyard are permitted to use that house, and the residents of that house itself do not need an eruv for this.
they do not change it. The eruv is not moved to another house.

for the sake of peace. The members of the house in which it is customary to place the eruv benefit by not having to give bread, and therefore they do not want the existing arrangement changed (Commentary to the Mishnah Gittin 5:8).
if they were many. More than eighteen (above, halacha 9).
in the airspace of the alley. In the alley itself, and not in one of the courtyards of the alley.
he must raise the vessel a handbreadth off the ground. It must be placed in a spot raised above the ground.
if they divided the eruv... it is not an eruv. Because the purpose of the eruv is to unite the domain of the residents of the courtyard (above, halacha 6).

so that children not forget the law of eruv. Although by law, residents who joined together in the alley need not make an eruv for the courtyards, since the alley partnership benefits the courtyards, the Sages decreed that even in this case the courtyards must make an eruv, because the children in the courtyard are not aware of the partnership placed in the alley and might think that carrying is permitted without an eruv (and see below 5:13-14).

for children recognize bread. Because bread is an essential staple of human life, the children notice that the residents of the alley joined in it, and there is no concern that they will think that carrying is permitted without an eruv.
and the day has become holy upon them. Shabbat has begun.
bread on the table may be relied on for the eruvei chatzerot. The bread of the meal can serve as the eruv of courtyards, since all of them are partners in it.
even though they are reclining in the courtyard. For unlike the eruv of courtyards, it is permitted to place the partnership in the courtyard (above, halacha 17).
one must acquire it for them through another. For the food to be acquired for the residents of the courtyard or alley, a person who is not the owner must acquire it on their behalf.
and he may. He is permitted.

but not through his son... because their hand is like his hand. They cannot acquire on behalf of others because they have no property of their own; whatever they acquire is considered his own acquisition.

in a matter that is by rabbinic law. And therefore she can acquire on behalf of others an eruv, which is by rabbinic law (above, halacha 2), although generally a minor does not acquire on behalf of others (Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 4:7).
and one may act on behalf of a person in his absence. An act that is solely to a person's benefit may be performed for him even without his knowledge (see also ibid. 4:2).
twilight. The time of dusk.

even though it is doubtfully day and doubtfully night. And although this time is generally treated stringently as Shabbat and work is forbidden in it (Hilchot Shabbat 5:4), they were lenient to make eruvei chatzerot and shittufei mevo'ot even at twilight (but one does not make eruvei techumin at the outset, below 6:13).
a heap. A collapse of stones.
terumah that became impure. Which is forbidden to eat (Hilchot Terumot 7:3).
in a cabinet. A chest.
unless he performed a labor at twilight. Specifically a labor forbidden by Torah law; but if he can take it out by a labor forbidden only by rabbinic law, it counts as an eruv (see also below 6:10).

he separated terumat ma'aser or great terumah and stipulated about it etc.. A person who separated terumah and at the time of separation stipulated that the terumah take effect only from nightfall (see also below 6:16; for the law of conditional terumah see Hilchot Terumot 4:7).
for throughout twilight it is still tevel. And one may not make an eruv with tevel (above, halacha 15).
the one who did not make an eruv relinquished his domain to them. And thereby transferred his domain to them, and they are permitted to carry, since there is no one to forbid it to them.
one who relinquishes his domain without specifying. And did not specify which domain.
for the heir stands in the place of the one he inherits from for every purpose. Just as the deceased could relinquish his domain on Shabbat, so too the heir (see also below, halacha 7).
and we do not say they should be like guests with him. And be permitted to carry, like an individual who relinquished his domain and became like a guest of those who relinquished (above, halacha 1).
and those who did not make an eruv are forbidden. Since they are many, they are not considered guests of those who made the eruv.

and those who made the eruv cannot relinquish their domain to two... for each of them forbids the other. These two who did not make an eruv forbid each other, since they neither made an eruv nor relinquished a domain.
for at the time the eruv-makers relinquished to him, he was forbidden. To carry in the courtyard because of his neighbor who did not make an eruv.

one who made an eruv does not relinquish his domain to one who did not. For example, if there were three residents and two of them made an eruv between them and the third did not, neither of the two can relinquish his domain to the one who did not make an eruv, since his fellow forbids it to them.

but the one who did not make an eruv relinquishes his domain to one who did. In this case, the eruv-maker to whom it was relinquished is permitted, while his fellow who made the eruv with him is forbidden, since no one relinquished a domain to him (Merkevet ha-Mishneh).

they relinquish from courtyard to courtyard. Two courtyards open to each other: the residents of one may relinquish their domain to the residents of the other, and the residents of the other are permitted to carry in both courtyards.
how so. They relinquish, then retract, and relinquish again.

and relinquishing a domain applies in a ruin just as in a courtyard. Two houses that open onto a ruin and forbid each other (below 3:17) may relinquish their domains and be permitted to carry, just as householders in a courtyard may relinquish their domains to one another.
and again carried in the domain he had relinquished. And thereby showed that he is retracting his relinquishment.
for he did not stand by his relinquishment. For the act of carrying out shows that he retracted his relinquishment.
they were first and took possession and carried out. They performed an act of taking possession by carrying vessels out into the domain that he relinquished to them.
two houses on two sides of the public domain. They cannot make an eruv between them because the public domain separates them.
and gentiles surrounded them with a partition on Shabbat. Thereby the houses became one domain and forbid each other from carrying from the house to the area between them without an eruv.

since it was impossible for them to make an eruv from the evening. The time of twilight is what determines the matter of the eruv (above 1:21), and since it was not possible to make an eruv at that time, it is no longer possible.
one of the residents of a courtyard. Who made an eruv with the other residents of the courtyard.
and left his domain to someone from the marketplace. Who did not make an eruv with the residents of the courtyard.

if he died while it was still day... he forbids them; and if he died after nightfall, he does not forbid them. The effect of the eruv takes hold at the start of Shabbat, and if at that time the residents of the courtyard were joined in an eruv and permitted to carry, they are permitted for the whole of Shabbat, even if others who did not join the eruv with them joined them during Shabbat (see below 3:25).
until the one he inherits from relinquishes his domain to them. As above, halacha 2.
an Israelite and a convert who dwell in one cave. And made an eruv between them.
and the convert died while it was still day. The law of a convert with no heirs is that whoever first takes possession of his property acquires it (Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 1:6).

even though no other Israelite took possession of his property until nightfall, this one who took possession forbids. Although at the start of Shabbat there was no one forbidding the Israelite, since it was possible to take possession of it while it was still day, the other person forbids even if he took possession after nightfall.
for he is like an heir. See above, halacha 2.

and if the convert died after nightfall... he does not forbid him. At nightfall the Israelite did not yet hold the property, and since at that time the convert did not forbid the Israelite with him (for they had made an eruv together), his domain remains permitted for the whole of Shabbat.
a resident alien (ger toshav). A gentile who lives in the Land of Israel and accepted upon himself to observe the seven Noahide commandments (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:6).
and they have already forbidden being alone with a gentile. Hilchot Rotzeach 12:7.

or the Israelites relinquished to one another and became like one individual with the gentile, it does not help at all. They are not permitted like a single individual dwelling with a gentile (in the previous halacha), because the permission there stems from the fact that it is uncommon for a single person to live with a gentile, but for many who relinquished to one another and became like one, this reason does not apply.
as if he were a guest with them. And he does not forbid them, as above, halacha 1.
two courtyards, one inside the other. To reach the inner courtyard one must pass through the outer courtyard.
he forbids the outer one until he rents from him. The gentile forbids until the Israelite of the outer one rents his domain from him.
for the feet of two Israelites and a gentile are found there. All of them tread and pass there.
and the inner one is permitted in the inner. Since no other Israelites live there, there is no one to forbid it to him (see below 4:19).
one may rent from a gentile even on Shabbat. Although ordinary renting is forbidden on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 23:12).
even for less than a perutah's worth. An amount of no value.
and a gentile's wife... and likewise his hired worker and his attendant may lease out without his knowledge. Even though the house is not theirs.

he became a partner with him in his domain and may lease it out without his knowledge. The right of use that the Israelite has in the gentile's domain makes him a partner in the house, and therefore he can lease out the house without his knowledge.
the first. The lessor.
if the second was not present. The lessee is not there.
they are permitted to carry from house to house through the windows. For the gentile's domain forbids them only to carry through the courtyard, but not through the windows.

for many do not become like one individual through an eruv in a place with a gentile. As above, halacha 10; therefore even though they made an eruv and became like one, they do not have the law of an individual living with a gentile, and they are forbidden to carry (and see also below 5:18).
publicly. In the open.
the minim. Heretics (for details see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:7).
Sadducees and Boethusians. People who challenge the tradition and authority of the sages of the Oral Torah (see ibid. 3:8, Hilchot Mamrim 3:3).

if they wish... all may make one eruv, the choice is theirs... and if they wish they make two eruvs. When two connected domains must make one eruv; and if there is a complete partition between them, they make two eruvs; and when there is a partition with a convenient passage between them, they may make one eruv or two.
but one between two houses, even if it is above ten. Since in a house one uses the space up to the height of the ceiling, even if it is above ten.
a window between a house and an upper room. An opening between the house and the attic (a second story).
a round window, if it can fit a square of four by four. If, along the circumference of the window, a square of four handbreadths by four handbreadths can be fitted.
a straw store. A storehouse for straw.
they make one eruv and do not make two. For they are considered one courtyard.

and even if the ladder was upright and leaning against the wall etc.. Even if the ladder stands parallel to the wall in such a way that one cannot climb it without moving its bottom away from the wall, the courtyards may make an eruv together if they wish.
if less than three remains between them. That the ladder reaches to within less than three handbreadths of the top of the wall.
if the wall was four wide. Its thickness is four handbreadths.
even though the ladders are far apart... they make one. Since the wall is wide and one can easily walk from ladder to ladder.
if there are not three between the ladders, they make one. Since the distance between the ladders is very small and can be crossed easily even though the wall is narrow.
he built a ledge on top of a ledge. A kind of shelves that project from the wall and can serve as steps.

if the lower one has four, it reduces. If the area of the lower ledge is four by four handbreadths, it reduces the height of the wall, and if from it to the top of the wall is not ten handbreadths, they may make an eruv together.
the lower one does not have four and there are not three between it and the upper one. When the difference in height between them is less than three handbreadths
,. The area of the lower and upper shelves are combined, and if together they have four handbreadths, they reduce.
and a projection. A protrusion jutting out of the wall.
he places a ladder in front of the projection. He leans the ladder on the projection.
and they make one if they wish. In this case one can easily pass from courtyard to courtyard by climbing the ladder to the projection and from it over the wall.

but if he placed the ladder beside the projection, it does not reduce. In this case it appears that the ladder is only meant to enlarge the projection and not to climb it, and so the use of the projection is to place objects on it and not to stand on it, and therefore it does not reduce (explained according to the Gemara).
he needs two projections, one not opposite the other. So that he can climb easily from the lower projection to the upper one.
a palm tree that he cut and leaned on the top of the wall and on the ground. He placed the piece of palm so that it serves as a kind of ladder.
and he need not fix it in a structure. Attach it to the wall and the ground.
its heaviness fixes it. Its great weight makes it considered fixed and attached to the ground.
straw. A pile of straw.
that has nothing to lean on. The ladder leans on an object that is not stable.
if the ladder was in the middle and straw on this side and straw on that side. The ladder leans on a strong partition and on both sides the partition is made of piles of straw.
and made it a ladder for the wall. That he uses it to climb the wall.

since it is the rabbinic prohibition that prevents him from climbing the tree. The prohibition of climbing a tree on Shabbat is a rabbinic decree (Hilchot Shabbat 21:6), and therefore they may make an eruv together, since the eruv takes effect at twilight (above 1:21), when they did not decree a shevut prohibition where a mitzvah is involved (Hilchot Shabbat 24:10, and see also below 6:9), and the eruv is for a mitzvah purpose (below 6:6).
an asherah. A tree used for idol worship.
for it is forbidden to benefit from. Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:11.
if the length of the reduction is four handbreadths. Along the length of the wall.
he demolished part of the wall. He broke off part of the wall's thickness.
until it was reduced below ten. On its side facing one of the courtyards.
its short side. The part lower than ten.
they assign it to this courtyard. To the courtyard next to the lower side.
and the rest of the high wall is between the two courtyards. And it has the law of a wall between two courtyards, as below, halacha 18.
the high wall between them was breached. A wall between two courtyards ten handbreadths high or more, that was breached.
because it is like a doorway. See also Hilchot Shabbat 16:16.
they make one eruv and do not make two eruvs. Because of the breach, the two courtyards are considered one courtyard.
he cuts into the wall a height of ten handbreadths. He makes an opening in the wall ten handbreadths high, along the length needed to complete the breach to ten cubits.
and if he wants to breach it at the outset. Where there was no breach at all.
the height of the breach must be his full stature. So that it is a passage that one can go through easily without stooping.
for if one fills a ditch with earth and pebbles, they are nullified. For a person intends to leave them there, and therefore they are considered part of the ground and reduce the depth of the ditch.
straw or hay do not reduce. For a person intends to take them from there, and therefore they are not considered part of the ground.
until he nullifies. Decides to leave them there.
that he extended it. Placed it.
they do not reduce with it unless he attached it to the ground. As long as it is not firmly attached to the ground, it is not considered part of the ground but an object lying on the ground.
a connection that cannot be removed without digging with a spade. A strong attachment that cannot be loosened without using a digging tool.

if he placed a board four handbreadths wide across the width of the ditch, they make one eruv. Since the board is wide and one can easily cross over it from side to side, it is considered a connection between the sides and they may make an eruv together.
two balconies, one opposite the other. Two balconies that stand facing each other.
if there are less than three handbreadths between them. The difference in height between them is less than three handbreadths.
higher than ten handbreadths from this courtyard and level with the ground of the second courtyard. For example, where the courtyards are built at two different levels.
by lowering. By means of a rope and the like.

one may not bring in from the thickness of this wall into the houses, and one may not take out from the houses onto its thickness. But it is permitted to bring in from the top of the wall into the courtyards or vice versa even without an eruv (as below 18-19).
a ruin. A ruined building.
because it is lower than it. The ruin is lower than the house.
enclosures that were fenced not for the sake of dwelling. Places that were surrounded by partitions for various uses other than dwelling.

none of which is more than a beit se'atayim. The area of the enclosures is less than the measure of a beit se'atayim (about 1150 square meters), and carrying in them is permitted on Shabbat (see Hilchot Shabbat 16:1).

alleys that have a side-post or a beam. Lanes leading off the public domain at whose entrance they placed a side-post (a post ten handbreadths high) or a beam, and carrying in them is permitted (ibid. 17:2).
a cistern. A water pit.
a partition ten handbreadths high. That divides the cistern between the two courtyards.
and where do they place the partition etc.... so that the domain of one is distinguishable from the domain of the other. So that the two courtyards can be distinguished.
as if it separated this part from that part. The beam is considered as dividing the cistern into two parts.

it is a lenient matter that the Sages were lenient regarding water. Although there is no complete partition here, the Sages were lenient regarding water to treat such a partition as a complete partition (see also Hilchot Shabbat 15:13).
a well in the middle of the path between two walls of courtyards. And they draw water from it through the windows.
distant. Far away.
and they need not extend projections over it. They need not make a projection jutting from the wall over the well as a marker (see Hilchot Shabbat 15:20).

for a person does not forbid his neighbor through airspace. People who use the airspace of a domain but do not enter it (such as in this case, where they draw water through the windows) do not forbid one another to carry without an eruv.
a small courtyard that was breached entirely into a large courtyard while it was still day. The wall of the small courtyard that it shares with the large courtyard was breached completely.
for posts remain to them on both sides. And by these posts it is evident that the courtyard stands on its own.

for the residents of the large one are considered in the small one etc.. From the standpoint of the residents of the small courtyard, the residents of the large courtyard are considered as living with them in the same domain and forbid them, but from the standpoint of the residents of the large courtyard, the residents of the small courtyard are in a separate domain (for this principle see also Hilchot Tefillah 8:7-8, Hilchot Kil'ayim 7:19).

since it was permitted for part of Shabbat, it is permitted for all of it. Since at the start of Shabbat the courtyards were permitted for carrying, they remain permitted for the whole of Shabbat despite the changes that occurred during Shabbat.
up to the base of the partition. The place where the partition stood.

for residents who arrive on Shabbat do not forbid. Residents who were added to the courtyard during Shabbat do not forbid the residents of the courtyard to carry, even though they did not make an eruv with them.
the window was opened etc.. Refers to the first case in the halacha, where the doorway or window was blocked on Shabbat.
they returned to their permitted status. And are permitted to carry between the courtyards.
and they were separated. They were divided.

it is forbidden to carry from one to the other, even if they were surrounded by a partition. For example, if they were surrounded by curtains, which is a loose connection (see Commentary to the Mishnah Shabbat 11:3).
like the house in which the eruv is placed etc.. Above 1:16.
five who collected the eruv etc.. Five residents of one courtyard who made an eruv for their courtyard.
when they carry it. When they carry a loaf in order to make an eruv with another courtyard.
for since they all collected, they became like members of one household. So their law is to give one loaf (above 1:16).
their master. Their employer.
but they eat at his table in payment for work they do for him. In return for work they do on his behalf.
or as a favor. That he does them a kindness and feeds them.
for known days. For a certain period and not on a regular basis.
like one who dines with his friend for a week or a month. This is an example of a person who dines for a certain time and not regularly.

if no other residents are with them in the courtyard they need not make an eruv etc.. When they are alone they are considered members of one household, but when other residents are with them they are not considered members of one household, since they do not always eat at one table.
in a large hall. A big hall.
a gatehouse. A room through which one enters the house.
they tread in it. They pass through it.
a portico. An open area in front of the house that has three walls and a roof.
a balcony. A platform raised above the courtyard, from which steps lead up to the upper floors (Commentary to the Mishnah Eruvin 8:3).
a storehouse. A warehouse.
a residence in which he relies to eat his bread. A place meant for dwelling in which he is accustomed to eat his meals.

if he set himself a place to eat in a gatehouse... it does not forbid it to him because it is not a residence. But if he set a place to eat in the cattle shed, the straw shed, the wood shed, or the storehouse, it forbids, because these are considered a residence (for the distinction between these places see also above 1:16, Hilchot Mezuzah 6:7).
since many tread in them. The members of the inner house and the one next to it who pass through them to reach their houses.
the ninth. The house adjacent to the innermost house.
many do not tread in it. Only the members of the inner house pass through it.
for each of them placed the eruv in the gatehouse of the other courtyard. And one who places his eruv in a gatehouse has not made an eruv (above 1:16).
and likewise a minor. Who has his own house.
as we have explained. Above 2:1.
even if it was adjacent to his courtyard. And he can return to it during Shabbat.
he removed his heart. He put it out of his mind.
he does not forbid them. Since he does not intend to return, he is not considered a resident of the courtyard who forbids the other residents of the courtyard.
until they rent his place from him. As above 2:10.
for it is possible that he will come on Shabbat. And therefore he is considered as if he were in the courtyard.
a hold of the hand. A right of use.
tevel. Produce from which terumah and tithes have not been separated, which is forbidden to carry.

in the whole courtyard and in everything considered together with the courtyard. All places that are considered one domain with the courtyard, such as the roofs of the houses and the walls between the courtyards (see above 3:18-19).
an upper room. An attic, a second story.
in the whole balcony and everything considered with it. As he goes on to explain in the next halacha.
for they are equal to it. In height, and it is more convenient for the residents of the balcony to use the mound than for the residents of the courtyard.
a ledge. A bench, a raised platform.

the balcony does not forbid the residents of the courtyard, for it is separated from them. The ledge serves as a partition between the balcony and the courtyard, and therefore they do not forbid each other (Maggid Mishneh). Some explain that it refers to the mound, that since the ledge separates the balcony from the mound, the residents of the balcony do not forbid the residents of the courtyard from using the mound (Merkevet ha-Mishneh).
projections. Protrusions.

and they may not use them with vessels that are in the houses. The residents of the courtyard and of the upper room are forbidden to place on the projections vessels that were kept in the house over Shabbat.
and its rim. The raised edge of the cistern that surrounds it.

it and its rim are like a rock or a mound in the courtyard. Since it is full to its brim with tevel, which is forbidden to carry, its only use is to place things on it, and its law is like that of a rock or a mound.
next to the balcony. Within less than four handbreadths (above, halacha 16).
but if it was full of water etc.. Since it is permitted to draw water from the cistern on Shabbat, the water level may drop below ten handbreadths.
and they pass over the outer one. They pass through the outer courtyard in order to enter and leave their courtyard.

and the outer one because of those who did not make an eruv who pass over them. Residents of a courtyard who are forbidden to carry in their courtyard forbid another courtyard through which they pass (as below, halacha 23).

one of the residents of the inner one forgot and did not make an eruv, both are forbidden. The inner one is forbidden because of that one who did not make an eruv, and the outer one is forbidden because the eruv is in the inner one.
for we have explained that one relinquishes from courtyard to courtyard. Above 2:5.

the outer one is forbidden and the inner one is permitted in its place. The residents of the inner one are permitted because they made an eruv and the eruv is placed in their courtyard, and the residents of the outer one are forbidden because one of them did not make an eruv.

they need not make an eruv; each of them uses his whole courtyard. For each of them is permitted in his courtyard since he is an individual, and therefore he does not forbid his fellow, according to the rule explained in the next halacha.

and if there was a gentile in the inner one, even though he is one, he is like many. The Gemara explains the reason: people might err and think that more than one gentile lives in the inner courtyard (and for an Israelite this concern does not exist, since they will assume that the residents of the inner one made an eruv with those of the outer one).
and many in each courtyard of them. For there are many residents in each courtyard.
the outer ones. Those at the sides of the inner one.
for many tread in the outer one. For the resident of the inner courtyard and the resident of the middle courtyard pass through the outer courtyard to reach their courtyards.
for each of them is permitted in his place. For he is an individual and does not need to make an eruv.

a foot that is forbidden in its place forbids not in its place etc.. Residents of a courtyard who are forbidden to carry in their courtyard forbid another courtyard through which they pass, and residents of a courtyard who are permitted in their courtyard do not forbid another courtyard through which they pass.
balconies. Gezuztrot, a kind of porch.

even if each of them made a partition ten handbreadths high etc.. A partition that descends from the balcony and extends opposite the water, so that it is considered as if the partition descends to the water and the water is in the same domain together with the balcony (see also Hilchot Shabbat 15:15).
because they are like one balcony. Since they are close in height they are considered one balcony, and therefore they must make an eruv together.
the upper one is permitted to draw and the lower one is forbidden. And the lower one does not forbid the upper one, since the bucket of the lower one does not pass through the upper one.
and if the residents of the lower one joined the residents of the upper one in the partition they made. They made the partition jointly.
porches. Balconies.

for one does not lower from domain to domain through a domain. Even though the upper and lower belong to the same person, he may not lower from the upper to the lower through the middle one, which is not his.
a pit. A hole.
those who made a pit, they pour slops into their own pit. Which is considered their domain.
an alley. A lane leading off the public domain onto which a number of courtyards open.

one kind. Although a partnership of courtyards need not be of one kind (above 1:11), in this case, since they are not joining for Shabbat but relying on their partnership in goods, they must be partners in one kind so that their partnership will be recognizable.
and in one vessel. See above 1:18.
they compel him. The court.
a storehouse. A warehouse.
with their knowledge. With their awareness and consent.

for they join only with their knowledge, since it is not a benefit to them. One may perform an act of acquisition for a person without his knowledge only when it is solely to his benefit and not when it involves a possible loss (see Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 4:2, and below 5:23, 6:18).

perhaps in the other alley they wish to join. And although they can join with both alleys (see below, halacha 7), it may be that they do not want the residents of the other alley to use the courtyard, since the exit through the first alley suffices for them (Maggid Mishneh).
and if they joined in two kinds... and he must inform them. Since perhaps now they do not want to make an eruv with a mixture of two kinds (Merkevet ha-Mishneh).
neighbors were added... and he must inform them. To inform the new neighbors, in case they want to make an eruv with the other courtyard.
the one it is accustomed to forbids, and the one it is not accustomed to does not forbid. For the courtyard is considered open only to the place it is accustomed to enter and leave.
they push it toward the alley it is not accustomed to. They consider it as if its main opening is to the alley it is not accustomed to.
to an enclosure larger than a beit se'atayim. An area of a beit se'atayim (about 1150 square meters) fenced not for dwelling.

since it is forbidden to carry from a courtyard to that enclosure. For the enclosure (and likewise the valley) has the law of a karmelit, into which it is forbidden to carry from a private domain (see Hilchot Shabbat 16:1, 14:13).

for he relies on the opening designated for him. The main opening from his standpoint is the one open to the enclosure, which is designated for him and not shared by all the residents of the alley. Some explain that the reason is the amount of open air and the width of the place (Meiri).
it does not forbid them. Similar to the law of a courtyard, above 4:13.
a ledge. A bench, a raised platform.
and their law regarding relinquishing a domain is like the residents of a courtyard etc.. Explained above 2:1.
and we have already said. Above 4:1.
and they did not require an eruv in the courtyards... except so that children not forget. Above 1:19.

for the alley is to the courtyards as a courtyard is to houses. Just as a resident who did not make an eruv in a courtyard forbids the residents of the courtyard to carry in the courtyard but they are permitted to carry in the houses, so a resident who did not join in the alley forbids the residents of the alley to carry in the alley but they are permitted to carry in the courtyard.
if they are not particular... they rely on the partnership. The partnership takes effect only for residents of an alley who are not particular about one another (above, halacha 2).
their slice. Their food.
and they permit this to them only under pressure. For the Sages required making an eruv in the courtyards so that children not forget.
one may carry in it only within four cubits, like a karmelit. Hilchot Shabbat 14:1.
as if it were open only to houses without courtyards. For the courtyards are nullified with respect to the houses.
and therefore one may not carry in all of it. For an alley onto which houses and courtyards do not open is considered a karmelit even if it has a side-post and beam (see ibid. 17:7-8).
and if the residents of the courtyards did not make an eruv, they may carry in all of it etc.. Like the law of an alley, in which one may carry vessels that rested there over Shabbat (above 3:18).
like a courtyard in which they did not make an eruv. Above 4:15.
who rent from the gentile etc.. Above 2:12.
or the Sadducee relinquishes to them. Above 2:16.
a gentile and one Israelite do not need a partnership. Similar to the law of a courtyard (above 2:9).
and the law of one Israelite... is one law. Many who rely on one table are considered an individual (above 4:1) and therefore need not join with the gentile.
to a valley. An open field.
and even if the opening was small, four by four. And there would have been room to say that this opening is not significant.

even though he takes camels and wagons out through the opening in the alley. And there would have been room to say that this opening is the main one from his standpoint. [Note: in the manuscripts the reading is 've-karnot', missing a vav, and therefore it may be that Rambam read this word, which is foreign in origin, with a kamatz under the resh: 've-karnot'.]
for his intention is only on the opening designated for him that leads to the valley. The main opening from his standpoint is the one open to the valley, which is roomier than the courtyard.
if it was a beit se'atayim or less, he does not rely on it etc.. Since this enclosure is small in area, it is no more significant to the gentile than the alley.
an alley with gentiles on one side etc.. See above 2:15.
in a city. A town.
so that children not forget. As above 1:19.
owned by an individual. Belongs to one person.
but if it belonged to many... they do not make an eruv for all of it. The reason will be explained in the next halacha.

and this is for recognition, so that they know etc.. This recognition is needed specifically in an eruv of a city that has two openings through which many enter and leave because it is large, and there is a concern that people will not be aware that they made an eruv.
they pass through. They go through.
and it does not need a reservation. There is no need to leave in it one place that is not included in the eruv.
if all of them made one eruv. If all the residents of the city are joined in one eruv.

he need not inform them, for it is a benefit to them. In that they can carry in the whole city. But if the city is joined in several separate eruvs (see the next halacha), he cannot acquire the eruv on behalf of the residents of the city without their knowledge, because it is a detriment to them, since perhaps they want to make an eruv with another part of the city (see above, halacha 4).
and the law of one who forgot etc.. These laws were explained in chapters 2 through 4.
and if they built a ledge at the entrance of the alley, it does not forbid them. Similar to the law of an alley, above, halacha 11.

one who left the city on Shabbat eve etc.. A person is forbidden to go out on Shabbat beyond the boundary of his city, that is, two thousand cubits from the edge of the city (see Hilchot Shabbat 27:1). But he may establish his Shabbat residence on Shabbat eve outside the city, and then he measures the two thousand cubits from that place, as explained here.
food for two meals. This amount was explained above 1:9.
within the boundary. Within the boundary of the city, which is two thousand cubits outside the city.
and established his Shabbat residence there. He decided in his mind that he wished to establish his place of rest in that place.
and he may walk from the place of his eruv two thousand cubits in every direction. For his boundary is measured from the place where he put his eruv (see also Hilchot Shabbat 27:5-6).
toward the city. In the direction of the city.
but only to the end of his measure. To the place in the city that is two thousand cubits from his eruv (as will be explained in the next halacha).
swallowed up within his measure. Entirely included within the two thousand cubits from his eruv.
so that his whole measure ends up outside the city. The edge of the two-thousand-cubit boundary from his eruv is outside the city.
the completion of the two thousand. The distance that completes the two thousand cubits.
even if it was a large city etc.. Provided that he placed his eruv in a place that was enclosed for the sake of dwelling (see below 7:4).
like Nineveh. Which was an extremely large city (Jonah 3:3).
even a ruined city. In which no one lives any longer.
or a cave fit for dwelling. Even though no one actually lives in it.

he walks all of it and outside it two thousand cubits in every direction. He may walk two thousand cubits beyond the boundaries of the domain in which he placed his eruv (and not only from the place of his eruv).

he did nothing. His act has no meaning and he did not acquire a Shabbat residence at the place where the eruv was put, since in any case he acquired a Shabbat residence in the city by virtue of being in it.

in places that are joined to the city etc.. There are places adjacent to the city that, although outside it, are considered part of it for purposes of measuring the boundary (for details of these places see Hilchot Shabbat 28:1-3).
if he put his eruv outside the boundary, it is not an eruv. Because he cannot reach it (below, halacha 11).
bandits. Robbers.
anything with which one may join. Any food with which a shittuf mevo'ot can be made, that is, any food except water, salt, truffles, and mushrooms (above 1:8).
a relish. Food eaten together with bread.
enough to eat two meals with it. An amount eaten with bread in the quantity of two meals.
like the partnership. Above 1:10.

so that it will be possible for him to eat it at twilight. Twilight is the time of dusk when Shabbat begins and the eruv is acquired, and for the eruv to take effect it must be possible to eat it at that time.
for it is impossible for him to bring it out from a private domain to a public domain etc.. Hilchot Shabbat 12:8.

in a karmelit. A domain from which bringing in and taking out to a private or public domain is forbidden only by rabbinic law (for its definition see Hilchot Shabbat 14:4; for the force of its prohibition see ibid. halachot 11, 13).

they did not decree against it at twilight where a mitzvah is involved or in a time of need. For twilight is doubtfully day and doubtfully night and is treated stringently (Hilchot Shabbat 5:4), but rabbinic prohibitions are permitted to be violated at twilight for a mitzvah or in a time of need (see ibid. 24:10), and the eruv of techumin is made only for such needs (above, halacha 6).
in a cabinet. A chest.
if he can take it out without performing a labor. Forbidden by Torah law (although he must perform a labor forbidden by rabbinic law to take it out; see also above 1:22).
the branch. A twig.

a decree lest he pluck it. Plucking something from where it grows is forbidden by Torah law (Hilchot Shabbat 8:3). And although using something attached to the ground is forbidden as a shevut (see ibid. 21:9), they did not permit this prohibition because it is likely to lead him to violate a Torah prohibition (Maggid Mishneh).
and stuck. In the ground.
it is an eruv. For there is no prohibition in plucking things that are not attached to the ground.
he has four cubits at the place of his eruv. Four cubits at the place where the eruv is placed are defined as his domain, that is, two cubits on each side around the eruv.
at the end of the boundary. At a distance of two thousand cubits from his place.
within two cubits it is an eruv, as if he had not left his place. Because in this case part of the domain of the one who placed the eruv (two cubits on each side of the eruv) is within the boundary.
terumah and it became impure. And this terumah is forbidden to eat (Hilchot Terumot 7:3).
the acquisition of the eruv at twilight... for a doubtful eruv is valid. See above 1:21.
two said to him. To the messenger.
one made an eruv for him. One made an eruv for him.

both acquired an eruv; twilight is a doubt, and a doubtful eruv is valid. Although it would seem that one of the eruvs surely did not take effect, since if twilight is part of the day the first one's eruv did not take effect (because it did not yet exist at the entry of Shabbat, which is at the start of the night), and if twilight is part of the night the second one's eruv did not take effect (because it was placed after Shabbat began), both are valid, because a doubtful eruv is valid.
a heap. A collapse of stones.
without performing a labor. Forbidden by Torah law.
that it is permitted to take it out at twilight. Above, halacha 10.
and if a heap fell on it after nightfall it is an eruv etc.. For the eruv already took effect at twilight.

for it is not a proper meal. Since such terumah is forbidden to eat (Hilchot Terumot 12:2). And although the prohibition on eating results from doubt, since in practice he cannot eat it, he does not acquire an eruv.

he said: this loaf is ordinary today and consecrated tomorrow etc.. A person who consecrated a loaf and at the time of consecrating stipulated that the sanctity take effect only the next day may make an eruv with it, since as long as it is not consecrated it may be eaten.

but if he said: consecrated today and ordinary tomorrow. A person who consecrated a loaf so that it would be sacred for only one day and the next day return to being ordinary may not make an eruv with it, since it is not fit to eat until it is definitely ordinary, that is, after nightfall, and at twilight, which is the time of acquiring the eruv, it is still forbidden to eat.
if he separated terumah and stipulated about it etc.. See the explanation above 1:22.
because a cemetery is forbidden to benefit from. Hilchot Avel 14:13.

and since he wants the eruv to remain there after its acquisition, he is benefiting from it. Since he wants the food with which he made the eruv to remain after the eruv is acquired so that he can eat it, he is benefiting from the cemetery (but the acquisition of the eruv itself is not considered benefit, since it is like performing a mitzvah; Commentary to the Mishnah Eruvin 3:1).
in a beit ha-peras. A field in which a grave was plowed and it is not known where the bones of the dead person are (Hilchot Tumat Met 2:16).
even if he was a kohen. Who is forbidden to enter a beit ha-peras (Hilchot Avel 3:13).

for he can enter there in a flying cabinet. A chest suspended in the air; a kohen is permitted to enter there in this manner because a beit ha-peras does not defile one who overshadows it but only one who touches it (Hilchot Tumat Met 10:2).
or he blows and walks. He blows with his mouth the dust at the spot where he intends to walk in order to make sure there are no bones of the dead there (see Hilchot Korban Pesach 6:8).
to acquire for them through another. For the food to be acquired for them, a person who is not the owner must acquire it on their behalf.
even though he wanted it only after nightfall, it is an eruv. It is treated as if he wanted it from before nightfall (see below 8:7).
anyone who acquires on behalf of eruvei chatzerot. These people are detailed above 1:20.
so that he will take bread with it for him and make an eruv techumin for him with it. That he will buy bread for him with the money he gave him and make the eruv for him.

but if he gave to a shopkeeper or a baker and said: acquire for me with this coin, it is not an eruv. A person who gives money to a shopkeeper or baker intends to buy the food with the money, and since food is not acquired by giving money but by pulling it (Hilchot Mechirah 3:1), the eruv does not take effect.

and if he said: make an eruv for me with this coin etc.. Because the meaning of this language is that he appoints him as an agent to make the eruv for him and not that he intends to buy the food with the money.
and if he gave him a vessel... he is buying food and making the eruv with it for him. Because by giving the vessel he acquires the eruv by the law of exchange (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5).
a person may make an eruv techumin through his son etc.. On their behalf, since they are under his authority.
the master. Their father or their employer.
he may not send it by a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor. Since they lack understanding and cannot place the eruv for him.

nor by one who does not acknowledge the mitzvah of eruv. Such as a Samaritan or a Sadducee (Commentary to the Mishnah Eruvin 3:2; see above 2:16). Even if they place the eruv in the spot, they do not intend that it be for the sake of the mitzvah of eruv.

and if he sent it with one of these disqualified people to bring it to a qualified person... it is valid. For the essential thing is the placing of the eruv itself, and it does not matter how the eruv got there.

one who says to his fellow: make an eruv for me with dates, and he made it with dried figs... it is not an eruv. In all these cases the person was particular about the manner of making the eruv and does not want it done in another way.
just as one recites a blessing over eruvei chatzerot and shittufei mevo'ot. 'Blessed are You, Lord... concerning the mitzvah of eruv' (above 1:16-17).
and returned to his city. After Shabbat began, which is the time the eruv takes effect (above 6:12).

and this is the essence of eruvei techumin, to make an eruv with one's feet etc.. The basic way to acquire a Shabbat residence in a particular place is to be present there at the start of Shabbat, and the permission to make an eruv by placing food for two meals (above 6:1) is a leniency granted to the wealthy person, so that he need not go himself to the place where he wants to acquire his Shabbat residence.
and set out on the road. Went on his way.
for he resolved in his heart. He decided.

for a poor person, whom we do not burden to place an eruv. A poor person has no ability to send his eruv with another, and therefore they permitted him to make an eruv in this way and did not burden him to make an eruv with his feet.
or did not specify the place where he acquired his Shabbat residence. He did not define in his mind the exact place where he wants to acquire his Shabbat residence (explained below, halacha 5).
and he has only two thousand cubits in every direction from the place where he is standing at nightfall. For the place where he is at nightfall becomes his Shabbat residence.
one who stood while it was still day in a private domain and acquired a Shabbat residence there etc.. See also Hilchot Shabbat 27:4.
a place that was not enclosed for dwelling. A place that was surrounded by partitions not for residential use.
a mound or a hollow. A place ten handbreadths higher or lower than the ground, with an area of four by four handbreadths, which is considered a private domain (ibid. 14:1).

if it was a beit se'atayim or less... more than a beit se'atayim he has in it only four cubits etc.. A place with an area smaller than a beit se'atayim (about 1150 square meters) is a private domain, and a place with a larger area is considered a karmelit in which one may carry only within four cubits (ibid. 16:1).

and likewise if he placed his eruv in a place that was not enclosed for dwelling. The law of one who places his eruv in a place not enclosed for dwelling is the same as that of one who rests there with his feet, and he has only two thousand cubits beyond the four cubits of his eruv (see above 6:4).
and did not specify his place of residence. He did not define the exact place where he wants to rest.
at its trunk. Next to the base.

for there is not the measure of two places there, and part of his place is thus defined. Under the tree or the rock there is not enough area for two separate places of four cubits, and there is necessarily a defined portion in which he acquired his residence.
he hands over his Shabbat residence to an acquaintance. He appoints his acquaintance to acquire a Shabbat residence on his behalf.

they did not acquire a Shabbat residence etc.. The people of the city intended to acquire a Shabbat residence by placing an eruv in that place, and since the eruv was not placed there, they did not acquire a residence. The messenger, however, intended to acquire a Shabbat residence with his feet, and since he set out on the way he acquired a residence even though he did not actually arrive there before Shabbat began (as above, halacha 2).
this that we said. Above, halacha 2.
he came down from the upper room. The attic.

he need not say: my residence is in such-and-such a place. Unlike one who makes an eruv with food, who must recite a blessing over the eruv and say that he is acquiring a residence there (above 6:24).
who resolved in his heart. Decided in his mind.

a person may make two eruvs in two directions and stipulate etc.. Although his condition becomes clear only after the eruv has already taken effect, it is treated as though it had been clarified from before nightfall (see below, halacha 7, for the explanation).
but on a festival it is permitted to carry from domain to domain. See also Hilchot Yom Tov 1:4.
the two festival days of the diaspora. Outside the Land of Israel the festival is observed for two days (see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:21, 6:14, Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh 5:4-5).
when does this apply? To the two festival days of the diaspora. The Sages considered them two separate days, and therefore two eruvs can be made on them for two directions.

but on the two festival days of Rosh Hashanah etc.. Unlike the other diaspora festivals, the two days of Rosh Hashanah are considered one long day, and therefore he cannot make two separate eruvs on them (see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:24).

in a matter that is rabbinic, there is bererah. Bererah is treating a doubtful situation that will become clear in the future as if it is already clear now. In the case of the eruv, although he wanted it after nightfall, which is after the time the eruv takes effect (above 6:8), it is treated as though he wanted it from before nightfall, and therefore he may go. The rule is that in Torah law there is no bererah, and in rabbinic law there is bererah (see also Hilchot Yom Tov 5:21, Hilchot Terumot 1:21).

the eruv must be present in its place on the first night and on the second night. Although he uses the same eruv for both days, each day is a separate eruv and it must be in existence at the start of that day.
and he stays until dark. He remains there until nightfall.
and takes it in his hand and goes home, if it was the night of a festival. Since there is no prohibition of carrying and transferring from domain to domain on a festival (Hilchot Yom Tov 1:4).

and the next day he brings it to that place and leaves it there until dark. If it was a festival and he took it the day before. If it was Shabbat, he returns to the place where he put the eruv the previous evening.
and eats it if it was the night of Shabbat. For he cannot return it, since carrying and transferring from domain to domain is forbidden on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 12:8).
because they are two holinesses etc.. The two days are separate and each needs its own eruv.

if he made an eruv with his feet on the first, he must make an eruv with his feet on the second. And he cannot make an eruv on the second day with bread, since one does not acquire a Shabbat residence with bread on Shabbat or a festival (Rabbi Chaim ben Shmuel in the name of Rambam, cited in Yad Peshutah).

if he wished to make an eruv with his feet on the second, it is an eruv. For he may acquire a Shabbat residence at the outset with his feet on Shabbat and a festival, since an eruv with the feet is not considered the acquisition of a residence that is forbidden on Shabbat and a festival.

he must make the eruv with the same bread with which he made it on the first. For the eruv with bread was already acquired on the eve of the first day, and now he merely relies on the eruv that already exists (like one who makes an eruv for many Shabbatot, above, halacha 6).
Shabbat eve or after Shabbat. On Friday or on Sunday.

at the time when they sanctified the month on the basis of sighting. In the period when the Sanhedrin was in the Land of Israel, Rosh Chodesh was determined on the basis of witnesses who testified that they saw the renewed moon. From the time of the destruction of the Land of Israel and the end of the Sanhedrin, Rosh Chodesh is determined by a fixed calculation (Hilchot Kiddush ha-Chodesh 5:1-3). According to this calculation, the first of Tishrei never falls on Wednesday or Friday, and therefore Yom Kippur never falls on Shabbat eve or on the Sunday after Shabbat (ibid. 7:1).

they are like one day and one holiness. They are considered one long day since the prohibition of labor on them is the same, and therefore the eruv is acquired from the first night for both days, and it is enough that it exist at twilight of the first day only (Maggid Mishneh).
this that we said. Above, halacha 5.
for the mitzvah of the eruv is that it be a proper meal from while it is still day. The eruv takes effect only when it is made with food that can be eaten before nightfall (above 6:16).
for nothing remains to him in the western direction. See above 6:4.
a festival that falls on Shabbat eve does not make an eruv etc.. Since one does not acquire a Shabbat residence with bread on Shabbat or a festival (see above, halacha 9).

and if he forgot and did not make an eruv, he may make an eruv... and stipulate. This law that one may stipulate applies only in the time when they sanctified the month on the basis of sighting, but now that the calendar is set by calculation, one does not make an eruv conditionally (Hilchot Yom Tov 6:15, responsum of Rabbi Avraham ben Rambam 38, cited in Yad Peshutah).

he may make eruvei chatzerot on Thursday and on Shabbat eve and stipulate. As explained in the next halacha, through this condition it turns out that he certainly made the eruv on a weekday and not on the festival.

but not eruvei techumin. Although through the condition it turns out that he certainly did not make the eruv on the festival, they were strict to forbid this because in any case it looks like acquiring a Shabbat residence (Rashba). In eruvei chatzerot they were not strict, because there is no acquisition of a residence in it, but only a sharing of one's domain with others (following the Rif).

but on the two festival days of Rosh Hashanah, they are like one day. Unlike other diaspora festivals that are observed for two days out of doubt, the two days of Rosh Hashanah are considered one long day that is entirely holy, and therefore one cannot make an eruv on them conditionally (see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:24).
